cards.title: Each tablet keeps its own list of claimed tokens
cards.atAShow: A GM deletes a transaction. The engine frees the token, but every tablet that stays connected keeps refusing it as already scanned until someone reloads. A tablet that drops its connection during Reset All Scores comes back still holding the old claims, and refuses tokens the engine has cleared.
cards.whyItHappens: The engine decides which tokens are claimed, but each tablet holds a copy that only grows: added on scan, merged on reconnect, removed only when a scan fails. The engine's own messages also skip facts changed by another path, such as a team created by a scan.
cards.designTerms: The engine's transaction module should own the claimed-token fact. The seam leaks: the tablet's storage module re-implements the claim rule in a separate handler per message, so one fact has two implementations and no locality.

examples.text: GM deletes a transaction; every connected tablet keeps refusing the token as already scanned until it reloads.
A tablet that dropped its connection during Reset All Scores reconnects with its stale claims and refuses cleared tokens.
After a reload a tablet knows only its own claims; a rescan of another station's token shows success, then rejection.
A delete recomputes every team's score but the message carries one team's row; latent today.
A scan for a team nobody added creates the team silently; no team message reaches any tablet.
Session Details freezes Teams and GM Stations at the last full snapshot, because one message merges and one replaces.

cards.title: Nothing says what a game boundary clears or keeps
cards.atAShow: The GM ends the game and restarts the engine; the ended game comes back as the current one and player scans keep landing in it. When the game ends, a tablet that reconnects loses its history and the wall scoreboard goes blank. A once-only cue spent in game one stays spent in game two.
cards.whyItHappens: Game start, end, reset, engine restart, tablet reload and reconnect each have their own code in each component. No table says, per fact and copy, whether a boundary clears, keeps or re-fetches it, and no message announces a boundary; screens infer one from a changed session id.
cards.designTerms: The engine's session module should own each fact's lifetime at a game boundary. That interface does not exist: the game-boundary rule is spread across the session, cue-engine, reset and tablet modules, each a shallow implementation of one case, so a change has no locality.

examples.text: An ended game comes back after an engine restart as the current game, and player scans keep landing in it.
After the GM ends the game, a reconnecting tablet loses history, scans and Download Report; the wall scoreboard goes blank.
A once-only cue spent in one game stays spent in the next unless the GM ran a system reset between.
After a reload the tablet wipes the offline scans it just restored, reading the first message as a new game.
A system reset empties the engine's video queue to idle while VLC plays on, and the GM is told nothing.
A system reset sends no tablet a fresh snapshot; tablets keep the old game's data until a new session id arrives.

cards.title: Reconnect snapshot and live update are built apart
cards.atAShow: A GM reloads a tablet mid-game. The History badge stays hidden until the next scan, and a rebuilt admin panel can show the clock as --:-- until the next change. The device list flips between everyone ever and connected only, depending on which message came last.
cards.whyItHappens: For each fact the engine has one builder for the connect snapshot and another for the live message, and six places send the snapshot with hand-picked arguments. The tablet applies each by a different rule, and the restore path fires none of the events screens listen for.
cards.designTerms: Each fact's engine module should own one description of itself, serving snapshot and live push alike. The snapshot builder is shallow: its interface is a hand-passed list of every module, and five tablet adapters reshape its output, so the seam leaks both ways.

examples.text: After a reload the History badge stays hidden until the next scan; the restore path fires no event.
After a panel rebuild the first state push can be skipped and the clock shows --:--.
The device list alternates between everyone ever and connected only, depending on which message came last.
Six places send the full snapshot and disagree on which devices to include and which extra keys to add.
Snapshot and live shapes differ for clock and cues; five adapters reshape them, and the clock adapter drops unnamed fields.
A TV reloaded during a video shows its last overlay state, because the snapshot's display status is never read.

cards.title: A reply never says which request, final or stored
cards.atAShow: Player devices upload their queued scans while no game exists. The engine answers processed, stores nothing, and both devices delete the scans. A GM's scan that can never succeed comes back as a generic error, so the tablet replays it at every reconnect with a toast each time. A slow Reset System reports failure and the new game is skipped.
cards.whyItHappens: The engine answers before or without the write that makes the fact true, calls an unstored batch processed, returns some failures as a typed result and others as a generic error, and acknowledges commands by action name alone. Each device then decides for itself what a reply means.
cards.designTerms: The engine's reply module should own each request's outcome: which request, final or not, stored or not. That interface is split between a typed result and a generic error, so three client adapters each keep their own reply rule across the seam.

examples.text: Scan failures like no session or queue full come back as a generic error; the tablet replays them on every snapshot.
A batch arriving with no game is answered processed but stored nowhere; both player devices delete it.
A batch retried after an engine restart is stored twice; processed batches are remembered in memory for an hour.
A system reset slower than the tablet's five-second wait reports failure, and the follow-on create session is skipped.
A command ack carries only action, success and message, so two presses of one action resolve on the first reply.
One failed batch is dropped by the web scanner on any 4xx but kept forever by the ESP32.
